text:
Chapter 8


A little later, when Mrs. Wilkins and Mrs. Arbuthnot, completely free of any chores, wandered down the worn stone steps and under the pergola into the lower garden, Mrs. Wilkins said to Mrs. Arbuthnot, who seemed deep in thought,
"Don't you see that if someone else handles the planning, it sets us free?"
Mrs. Arbuthnot agreed, but she still felt it was a bit silly to have everything taken out of their hands.
"I love having things taken out of my hands,"
Mrs. Wilkins said.
"But we found San Salvatore,"
Mrs. Arbuthnot said,
"so it's a bit annoying that Mrs. Fisher is acting like it belongs only to her."
"What's really silly is caring about it,"
Mrs. Wilkins said calmly.
"I don't see any point in being in charge if it costs you your freedom."

Mrs. Arbuthnot didn't reply for two reasons. First, she was amazed by how calm and sensible the usually disorganized and hyper Lotty was becoming. Second, the view in front of her was absolutely breathtaking.

All along the stone steps, purple periwinkles were in full bloom, and Mrs. Arbuthnot could now see what had brushed against her wet face the night before. It was wisteria. Wisteria and sunshine... she remembered the ad. Here, they were both everywhere. The wisteria was overflowing with life and flowers. Where the pergola ended, the sun shone brightly on bushes of red geraniums, mounds of nasturtiums, burning-orange marigolds, and red and pink snapdragons, all competing in brilliant colors. The ground sloped down in terraces toward the sea, with each terrace acting as a small orchard. Olive trees grew alongside vines on trellises, fig trees, peach trees, and cherry trees. The cherry and peach trees were blooming, creating lovely clouds of white and deep pink among the delicate grey-green olives. The fig leaves were just beginning to smell like figs, and the grapevines were starting to bud. Beneath the trees grew clusters of blue and purple irises, lavender bushes, and prickly cacti. The grass was covered with dandelions, daisies, and wild onions, and at the very bottom was the blue sea. Colors seemed splashed everywhere without any plan, like rivers of paint—the periwinkles looked as if they were pouring down the sides of the steps. Flowers that were kept in neat, exclusive borders in England, like irises and lavender, grew right alongside common weeds like dandelions and daisies, looking even happier and healthier for it.

They stood in silence, looking at this beautiful, happy mess. No, it really didn't matter what Mrs. Fisher did. Not in a place as beautiful as this. Mrs. Arbuthnot's annoyance completely vanished. In the warmth and light of this place—which felt to her like a glimpse of a gentler, new side of God—how could anyone remain upset? If only Frederick were here with her, seeing it the way he would have when they were first in love, back when they shared the same thoughts and loved the same things...

She sighed.
"You shouldn't sigh in heaven,"
Mrs. Wilkins said.
"People don't do that here."
"I was just thinking how much you want to share this with the people you love,"
Mrs. Arbuthnot said.
"You shouldn't long for anything in heaven,"
Mrs. Wilkins said.

"You're supposed to be completely satisfied. And this is heaven, isn't it, Rose? Look how everything is allowed in together—the weeds and the fancy flowers, the ordinary and the elite, me and Mrs. Fisher. Everyone is welcome, all mixed up, and everyone is happy and enjoying themselves."
"Mrs. Fisher doesn't seem happy—at least, not outwardly,"
Mrs. Arbuthnot smiled.
"She will start soon, you'll see."

Mrs. Arbuthnot said she didn't think people changed or started new things after a certain age.

Mrs. Wilkins insisted that no one, no matter how old and stubborn, could resist such perfect beauty. In a few days, maybe even hours, they would see Mrs. Fisher open up.
"I'm sure we're in heaven,"
Mrs. Wilkins said,
"and once Mrs. Fisher realizes that, she will have to change. You'll see. She will stop being so stiff and rigid, and she'll soften up. We might even end up liking her."

The idea of Mrs. Fisher softening up—when she seemed so tightly locked in her ways—made Mrs. Arbuthnot laugh. She forgave Lotty's casual talk about heaven, because on a morning like this, forgiveness was in the air. Besides, they had every reason to feel that way.

Lady Caroline, still sitting on the wall where they had left her before breakfast, looked down when she heard laughter. Seeing them on the path below, she felt relieved that they were laughing down there instead of right next to her. She disliked jokes in general, but she hated them in the morning, especially when they were loud and close by. She hoped the two eccentrics were leaving for a walk rather than coming back. They were laughing louder now. What on earth could they find so funny?

She stared down at the tops of their heads with a very serious expression, worried about spending a month with people who laughed so much. As if they felt her stare, they suddenly turned and looked up.

Their constant friendliness was exhausting...

She tried to ignore their smiles and waves, but she couldn't move back without falling into the lilies. She didn't smile or wave back. Instead, she stared at the distant mountains until the two women, tired of waving, walked away around the corner and disappeared.

This time, they both noticed that they had been ignored.
"If we weren't in heaven,"
Mrs. Wilkins said calmly,
"I'd say we were snubbed. But since no one snubs anyone in heaven, that couldn't have been a snub."
"Maybe she's unhappy,"
Mrs. Arbuthnot suggested.
"Whatever is wrong, she'll get over it here,"
Mrs. Wilkins said confidently.
"We should try to help her,"
Mrs. Arbuthnot said.
"Oh, but no one needs help in heaven. That's all in the past. You don't have to try to do anything. You just exist."
Mrs. Arbuthnot decided not to argue about that today. Her vicar back home would have called Lotty's talk disrespectful or even blasphemous. From here, the vicar seemed so distant and old.

They left the path and climbed down the olive terraces, going lower and lower until they reached the warm, calm sea lapping gently against the rocks. A pine tree grew close to the water, and they sat under its shade. A green-hulled fishing boat floated motionless on the water. The ripples made soft, gurgling sounds at their feet. They squinted against the bright sunlight outside the shade of the tree. The warm scent of pine needles, wild thyme growing between the rocks, and the sweet smell of irises in the sun drifted past them. Soon, Mrs. Wilkins took off her shoes and socks and dipped her feet in the cool water. After watching her for a minute, Mrs. Arbuthnot did the same. Their happiness was complete. Their husbands wouldn't have recognized them. They stopped talking and ceased mentioning heaven. They simply sat, quietly enjoying the peace.

Meanwhile, Lady Caroline was sitting on the wall, thinking about her situation. The garden on top of the wall was lovely, but it was open to interruptions. At any moment, the others might walk in, since both the hall and the dining room opened directly into it. She wondered if she could claim this garden as her private space. Mrs. Fisher had the castle terrace, which was full of flowers, and a watchtower to herself, not to mention the best bedroom. The other two women could easily go elsewhere; she had noticed at least two other small gardens, and the entire hill was full of paths and benches. Why couldn't this one spot be reserved for her? She liked it best of all. It had the Judas tree, a pine tree, freesias, lilies, and a pink tamarisk bush. It had the low wall to sit on and incredible views on three sides: the bay and mountains to the east, the village across the green harbor and hills with white houses to the north, and the narrow strip of land connecting the castle to the mainland, the sea, and the coast toward France to the west. Yes, she would ask to have this garden to herself. It made perfect sense for each of them to have their own private area. It was essential for her to have quiet, alone time without being bothered. The others should prefer it too. Why crowd together? She had enough of that in England, with endless relatives and friends constantly surrounding her. Having successfully escaped them for a month, why would she want to crowd around strangers now?

She lit a cigarette, starting to feel relaxed. The other two had gone for a walk, and Mrs. Fisher was nowhere to be seen. It was very pleasant. But just as she took a deep breath of relief, someone came through the glass doors. Surely it wasn't Mrs. Fisher trying to sit with her? Mrs. Fisher had her terrace and should stay there. It would be very annoying if she wanted to claim this garden in addition to her private sitting room and terrace.
Thankfully, it wasn't Mrs. Fisher; it was the cook. She frowned. Was she going to have to keep planning the meals? Surely one of those two waving women would take over that chore now.

The cook had been waiting anxiously in the kitchen, watching the clock tick closer to lunchtime without knowing what to prepare. She had first gone to Mrs. Fisher, who had immediately dismissed her. She then searched the house for anyone who could tell her what to cook, but found no one. Finally, directed by Francesca (who always knew where everyone was), she came out to find Lady Caroline.

Domenico had hired this cook. Her name was Costanza, and she was the sister of one of his cousins who ran a restaurant down in the town square. She helped her brother cook when she didn't have other work, and she knew how to make all kinds of rich, traditional Italian dishes that local workmen and Sunday visitors loved. She was a thin, fifty-year-old single woman with grey hair, quick movements, and a lot to say. She thought Lady Caroline was the most beautiful person she had ever seen, and so did Domenico, his nephew Giuseppe, Francesca's niece Angela, and Francesca herself. Domenico and Francesca, who were the only ones who had seen the other two ladies, thought they were nice-looking, but compared to the beautiful blonde girl, they were like candles compared to the modern electric lights recently installed in the castle.

Lady Caroline scowled at the cook. As usual, her scowl looked more like a look of beautiful, serious thought. Costanza threw up her hands, calling on the saints to witness that this girl looked just like a painting of the Virgin Mary.

Lady Caroline crossly asked her what she wanted, but Costanza just tilted her head in delight at the musical sound of her voice. After waiting to see if she would say more, the cook explained that she needed menu orders. She had tried asking the young lady's mother, but without success.
"She is not my mother,"

Lady Caroline said angrily, though her anger sounded like the sweet, sad voice of an orphan. Costanza immediately began offering sympathy, explaining that she also had no mother. Lady Caroline interrupted to inform her briefly that her mother was alive and well in London.
Costanza thanked God and the saints that the young lady didn't know the pain of losing a mother. Misfortunes happened quickly enough, she said, and then asked if she had a husband.
"No,"

Lady Caroline said coldly. She hated the topic of husbands even more than morning jokes. Everyone was always trying to push her to get married—her family, her friends, and the newspapers. She could only marry one person, but from the way people talked (especially her suitors), you'd think she could marry a dozen.
Her soft, sad-sounding "No" filled Costanza with sympathy.
"Poor little one,"
Costanza said, actually patting her on the shoulder to encourage her.
"Don't worry, there's still time."
"For lunch,"
Lady Caroline said coldly, shocked that she was being patted by the cook when she had traveled all this way to escape such familiarity,
"we will have—"

Costanza interrupted with suggestions, which were all delicious and very expensive. Lady Caroline didn't realize they were costly and agreed to them immediately. They sounded very nice, involving fresh spring vegetables, fruits, lots of butter, cream, and a large number of eggs. Costanza enthusiastically remarked that she preferred cooking for English guests because they knew how to live well, didn't skimp on ingredients, and didn't try to underpay the locals.
Realizing she might have been too extravagant, Lady Caroline quickly cancelled the cream.
Costanza's face fell, since the cream was supposed to come from her cousin's cow.
"And maybe no chickens either,"
Lady Caroline said. Costanza looked even more disappointed, as her brother kept chickens at his restaurant and had several ready for sale.
"Also, don't order strawberries until I've talked to the other ladies,"
Lady Caroline said, remembering it was only the first of April and that the ladies from Hampstead might have a tight budget.
"I'm not the one running things here."
"Is it the old lady?"
Costanza asked, her face falling.
"No,"
Lady Caroline said.
"Which of the other two ladies is it?"
"Neither,"
Lady Caroline replied.
Costanza smiled again, figuring the young lady was just joking with her. She said so in a friendly way, looking delighted.
"I never joke,"
Lady Caroline said shortly.
"You had better go, or lunch won't be ready by twelve-thirty."
These abrupt words sounded so pleasant to Costanza that she felt complimented. She forgot all about the cream and chickens and walked away smiling and grateful.
"This will never work,"
Lady Caroline thought.
"I didn't come here to manage a house, and I'm not going to."
She called Costanza back. Costanza came running, thrilled to hear her name called in that voice.
"I have ordered lunch and dinner for today,"
Lady Caroline said with her serious, angelic expression,
"but from now on, you must go to one of the other ladies for orders. I won't be doing it anymore."

The idea of her managing the household was ridiculous. She never did that at home; no one would ever ask her to. It was silly that this chore was being dumped on her just because she could speak Italian. Let the other two ladies do it if Mrs. Fisher refused. Mrs. Fisher was obviously the one meant for it. She looked and dressed like a strict housekeeper, and even styled her hair like one.

She gave her final warning with a sharpness that sounded sweet anyway, waving her hand to dismiss her in a way that looked like a blessing. It was annoying when Costanza just stood there with her head tilted, looking at her with delight.
"Oh, go away!"
Lady Caroline exclaimed in English, suddenly losing her patience.

There had been a single fly in her bedroom that morning that had bothered her just like Costanza was doing. It was determined to land on her face, and she was determined to stop it. It woke her up and kept her from sleeping. Whenever she slapped at it, it easily dodged her, and she ended up hitting herself. It kept coming back, landing on her cheek with a loud buzz. She slapped at it again and hurt herself, while it flew away gracefully. She lost her temper, sat up, and tried to swat it with all her strength, treating it like an enemy trying to drive her crazy. But it slipped around her blows effortlessly and returned immediately. It always succeeded in landing on her face, completely unfazed by being shooed away. That was why she had dressed and come out early. She had already told Francesca to put a net over her bed, as she wasn't going to let that happen again. People were just like flies, she thought. She wished there were nets to keep them away too. She tried to swat them away with sharp words and frowns, but they dodged her words just like the fly. Unlike the fly, they didn't even realize she was trying to get rid of them. At least the fly left for a moment; with people, the only way to get rid of them was to leave herself. That was why she had come here in April. But now that she was here, she was finding that she couldn't escape the details of daily life or the people either. Back in London, San Salvatore had seemed like a quiet, empty paradise. But after just twenty-four hours, she realized it wasn't empty at all, and she was still having to defend her space. Mrs. Fisher had hovered around her almost all of yesterday, and this morning she hadn't had even ten minutes of peace.

Costanza finally had to go cook, but as soon as she left, Domenico arrived. He came to water and tie up plants. That was normal for a gardener, but he kept working right next to her, watering plants that didn't need it and tying up stems that were already straight. At least he was a man, so he was slightly less annoying. When he smiled and said good morning, she smiled back—and immediately, Domenico forgot his wife, family, and chores, and looked like he wanted to kiss her feet.

He couldn't do that, of course, but he talked constantly as he worked, gesturing so wildly that he had to set down his watering can, making the chore take even longer. Lady Caroline tolerated it for a while but eventually couldn't stand it. Since he wouldn't leave and she couldn't tell him to go while he was doing his job, she was the one who had to move.

She got off the wall and walked to the other side of the garden, where there were some comfortable cane chairs in a shed. She just wanted to turn one around so her back was to Domenico and she faced the sea. It was such a small thing to ask. But he was watching her closely, and as soon as she went toward the chairs, he ran over, grabbed one, and asked where she wanted it. Would she ever escape being waited on, being asked how to be made comfortable, and having to say thank you? She spoke curtly to Domenico, who immediately assumed the sun had given her a headache. He ran inside and brought her a parasol, a cushion, and a footstool, acting extremely helpful and polite.

She shut her eyes in resignation. She couldn't be mean to Domenico, and she couldn't just walk indoors like she would have with the others. Domenico was smart and very capable. She had quickly realized that he was the one who actually ran the castle and got things done. His manners were lovely, and he was a very pleasant person. It was just that she wanted so badly to be left alone. She felt that if she could just have one quiet month to herself, she might actually figure out what she wanted to do with her life.

She kept her eyes closed so he would think she was asleep and leave. Domenico thought she looked incredibly beautiful with her eyes closed. He stood there staring at her in silence. Thinking he had gone, she opened her eyes again. But no, he was still there, staring. Even him. She just couldn't escape being stared at.
"I have a headache,"
she said, closing her eyes again.
"It's the sun,"
Domenico said,
"from sitting on the wall without a hat."
"I want to sleep."
"Yes, signorina,"

he said sympathetically, and quietly walked away.

She opened her eyes with a sigh of relief. The glass doors clicked shut, showing that he had gone inside and left her in the garden to be undisturbed. Now, hopefully, she would be alone until lunchtime. It was strange, and no one was more surprised than she was, but she actually wanted to think. She had never wanted to do that before. She had tried almost everything else in life, but she had never sat down just to think. She had come to San Salvatore simply to lie in the sun for four weeks, away from her parents and friends, doing nothing but eating and sleeping. Yet she had only been here a few hours when this new desire to think took hold of her.

The stars had been beautiful the night before. After dinner, she had left Mrs. Fisher alone with her nuts and wine and gone out to the garden. Sitting on the wall near the white lilies, she had looked out into the dark night, and it suddenly felt as if her life had been a lot of meaningless noise. She was shocked by this thought. She knew that starry nights could make people emotional—she had seen it happen to others—but it had never happened to her before. A lot of noise about nothing. She wondered if she was getting sick. For a long time, she knew her life was hectic and loud, but she had always assumed it was important. Indeed, it was so loud that she felt she needed to escape for a bit before she went deaf. But what if it was all just noise about nothing?

She had never had a thought like that before, and it made her feel lonely. She wanted to be alone, but not lonely. Loneliness was different; it was a painful ache deep inside. It was what people dreaded most, and it was the reason she went to so many parties—though lately, even parties hadn't kept the loneliness away. Was it possible that loneliness had nothing to do with where you were, but only with how you felt? Perhaps, she had thought, she should just go to bed. She must not be feeling well.

She went to bed, but in the morning, after escaping the fly, eating breakfast, and coming out to the garden, the feeling returned in broad daylight. Once again, she had the uncomfortable suspicion that her life so far had been loud but empty. If her first twenty-eight years—the best years of her life—had been wasted on meaningless noise, she needed to stop and think about her future. She didn't have many blocks of twenty-eight years left. In another twenty-eight years, she would look like Mrs. Fisher. In two more blocks—she turned away from the thought.

Her mother would have been very worried if she knew. Her mother adored her, and so did her father. Everyone adored her. When she stubbornly insisted on going to Italy for a month with strangers she found in a newspaper ad, refusing even to bring her personal maid, her friends assumed that poor
"Scrap"

(as they called her) was just exhausted and having a nervous breakdown.

Her mother had been upset when she left. It was such a strange choice, suggesting she was unhappy. Her mother went along with the breakdown rumor. If she could have seen her beloved Scrap—who was more beautiful than any other daughter, her mother's pride and joy—sitting there staring at the Mediterranean at noon, thinking about her life blocks, she would have been devastated. Going away alone was bad enough; thinking was even worse. No good could come from a beautiful young woman thinking. It only led to complications, hesitation, and unhappiness. Yet here sat Scrap, thinking very deeply about serious things—the kind of things people didn't normally think about until they were at least forty.
